Alaska primary voters set stage for races down the stretch
JKT, Peltola lead respective races in primary
sources.text:
Three crowded races for Alaska’s governor, U.S. Senate and U.S. House races narrowed considerably after voters cast their ballots in Tuesday’s open primary election.
As of Tuesday night for the gubernatorial race, Democratic candidate Jonathan “JKT” Kreis-Tomkins, a former Sitka representative and his running mate Zac Johnson, had the lead with 21.7% of the vote, while former Anchorage Sen. Tom Begich, a Democrat, and his running mate, Julia Hnilicka, had 20% of the vote. Republican candidate Bernadette Wilson and her running mate Mike Shower claimed 10.5% and Republican former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and his running mate Josh Church had 8.4%.
The gubernatorial race had a field of 17 candidates.
In the U.S. Senate race, former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democrat, took an early lead with 48%, followed by Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Dan S. Sullivan with 42.8% of the vote. Retired Petersburg teach Dan J. Sullivan came in a distant third with 2.4%. Fairbanks resident David Leslie, a Democrat and Republican Gerald L. Heikes were tied at 1.1%, with 23 votes separating them. Sixteen candidates had entered the race.
Alaska’s U.S. Senate seat is one of the most expensive in the state’s election cycle, with incumbent Sullivan and Peltola raising and spending millions. Peltola’s campaign reported raising $8.7 million through the second quarter of this year, while Sullivan raised $4.2 million and is maintaining an $8 million war chest.
Alaska’s at-large U.S. House seat saw Republican incumbent Rep. Nick Begich leading with 46.1%, followed by Bristol Bay independent Bill Hill with 31%. Anchorage pastor Matthew Schultz, a Democrat who suspended his race to support Hill, followed in third with 8.1% and Eric Hafner, another Democrat who is an inmate in a New York federal prison, received 3.8% of the vote. Fifteen candidates, including Republican, Democratic and independents, filed for the seat.
As of 1:48 a.m. Wednesday, 378 of the state’s 403 precincts had reported results.
Ballot Measure 1, which would establish campaign contribution restrictions, was overwhelming trending toward passing, with 71.5% voting yes and 28.5% voting no.
If Measure 1 passes, it would cap contributions from individuals to $2,000 and $5,000 for political parties. Individuals could donate up to $4,000 for joint governor/lieutenant governor campaigns, while political parties could provide up to $8,000. The amount would be adjusted for inflation every 10 years starting in 2031.
Fairbanks area residents hit their polling places on Tuesday to cast their ballots. At the Tanana Valley State Fairgrounds, precinct chair Valerie Therrien said there was a steady flow of voters.
“I’m impressed,” she said. She said 175 voters had cast their ballot by 12:30 p.m.
Chad Rankin, a poll watcher, was busy observing how polling staff were handling voters.
“They’ve been very effective,” Rankin said of the election workers. “They’ve helped people and are taking care of everyone they can legally.”
Voters had different reasons that brought them out to the polls.
For resident Tom McCann, it was simple. “Build the Line,” he said, referring to the campaign slogan urging state lawmakers to back measures to build the proposed Alaska LNG project.
“We need cheap energy and we need it to create jobs and put people to work,” McCann said. McCann said he didn’t vote for some incumbents “because they didn’t get the job done pushing the Alaska LNG pipeline through.”
McCann said he wasn’t too fond of Alaska’s current open primaries and ranked-choice general election system. He said primary candidates should be determined by parties, not by what he considered a free-for-all.
Retired teacher Myra Helmer said she wants whoever gets elected to prioritize education.
“We used to be among the best in the country,” Helmer said. Now Alaska education ranks toward the bottom nationally.
“It’s a shame that schools have to beg and borrow to get funded,” Helmer said, noting years of flat funding and advocacy to secure state funding. She added that strong educational programs are part of what ensures Fairbanksans and their families remain in or return to the community.
A 58-year resident of Fairbanks, Helmer said she’s never missed voting and noted every eligible Alaska voter should cast their ballot.
“My observation is that if you don’t vote and you’re gathered around the dinner table later, you don’t have a leg to stand on if you didn’t put your two cents in at the polls,” Helmer said.
All of the candidates for Interior Alaska’s state legislative seats will go on to the Nov. 3 ranked-choice general election unless they withdraw from the race.
In Senate District Q, which includes North Pole, Eielson and the east half of Badger Road, Republican Frank Tomaszewski led with 62.3% of the vote to North Pole independent William Hunter’s 37.7%. Frank Tomaszewski filed to run for the Senate seat after incumbent Sen. Robb Myers (R-North Pole) announced he would not run on the last day to file.
For House District 31, which includes downtown Fairbanks, Democratic incumbent Rep. Maxine Dibert netted 58.3% of the vote to Republican Aimee Moore’s 37.1%. Libertarian Jonathan Powell-Mark came in third with 4.6%.
House District 32 incumbent Rep. Will Stapp (R-Fairbanks) is running unopposed on the ballot for the 2026 election.
In House District 33, which covers North Pole and East Badger Road, Republican incumbent Rep. Mike Prax led with 38.1% of the vote, followed by Republican challenger Barbara Haney with 34.5% and independent Pepper McFarland with 27.5%.
In House District 34, which includes Steele Creek, Two Rivers, Eielson and Salcha, independent Joy Beth Cottle came out ahead with 52% of the vote following early morning updates to Republican Harmony Tomaszewski's 48%. The seat was left open after incumbent Frank Tomaszewski filed to run for the Senate District Q seat. Harmony Tomaszewski is Frank Tomaszewski’s wife.
In House District 35, which covers west Fairbanks, Chena Pump and Ester, Democratic incumbent Rep. Ashley Carrick received 60.4% of the vote, followed by Republican Jeffrey Rentzel with 35.6% and independent Terra Bridger with 3.9% of the vote.
In House District 36, one of the state’s largest districts, which covers a swath of Interior Alaska, Tok, Delta Junction and Glennallen, Republican incumbent Rep. Rebecca Schwanke was ahead with 56.4%, followed by independent Crystal Jones with 43.6%. As of 1:50 a.m. on Wednesday, 38 of District 36’s 40 precincts reported in.
All election results are unofficial until certified. Election night results, along with all early voting ballots cast up to Aug. 14, were counted on Tuesday.
The Division of Elections must still count questioned and absentee ballots, which will be updated as they are counted through Aug. 28.
Editorial note: The results have been updated after post-print deadline to reflect latest unofficial Division of Elections reports.

sources.news_title: Senate Race Finally Called — Republican Majority On The Line
sources.text:
One of the most closely watched races of the 2026 midterm elections is beginning to take shape after voters delivered the first major decisions Tuesday night.
The result sets up a November contest that could attract enormous national attention as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of the United States Senate.
Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola advanced from Alaska’s unusual open primary Tuesday and will face each other in November’s four-way general election.
Sixteen candidates appeared together on the primary ballot regardless of political affiliation, with the top four finishers advancing to the general election under Alaska’s election system.
The identities of the other two candidates advancing had not yet been called, leaving open the possibility of an unusual complication involving another candidate who shares the incumbent senator’s name.
Republicans have accused Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg, of entering the contest to confuse voters and potentially siphon support away from Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.
Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. has rejected those accusations and maintained that his candidacy is legitimate.
The controversy has taken on greater significance because Alaska has emerged as a potentially important battleground in the fight for control of the Senate.
Sen. Sullivan is seeking a third term in a state President Donald Trump carried by more than 13 percentage points during the 2024 presidential election.
The Republican incumbent has raised more than $11 million and reported having more than $7 million available at the end of July.
Democrats, however, believe Peltola’s previous statewide success and history of breaking with her party could make the race considerably more competitive than Alaska’s presidential results might suggest.
Peltola represented Alaska’s at-large House district from 2022 until 2025 after becoming the first Alaska Native woman elected to Congress in a special election following the death of longtime Republican Rep. Don Young.
During her time in Congress, Peltola sometimes broke with Democrats on issues including energy development and border enforcement, and she is campaigning for Senate with an emphasis on Alaska’s fishing and energy industries.
Peltola has also demonstrated significant fundraising strength, bringing in more than $18 million and reporting more than $4.6 million in cash on hand at the end of July.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., recruited Peltola for the Senate contest after Democrats concluded that the former congresswoman offered them a strong opportunity to challenge Sullivan.
Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski previously endorsed Peltola during her 2022 and 2024 House campaigns but has endorsed Sullivan in this year’s Senate contest.
Money is already pouring into the contest, with more than $56 million spent on advertising connected to the Senate race, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.
But the second Dan Sullivan has added an extraordinary wrinkle to what was already expected to be an expensive campaign.
Sen. Sullivan accused Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. of being a Democratic plant after the retired teacher entered the race in June, pointing to his lack of a background in Republican politics and reported connections to people who previously supported Democratic candidates.
Republicans unsuccessfully attempted to have Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. removed from the ballot, arguing that his candidacy was undertaken in bad faith.
Peltola has denied having any connection to Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.’s campaign.
The controversy has now reportedly attracted federal scrutiny, with NBC News reporting Tuesday that a grand jury issued subpoenas as investigators examine whether Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy was legitimate.
An attorney who represented Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. during the earlier ballot dispute said his client had not received a subpoena and that the attorney was unaware of a federal investigation involving him, The Washington Post reported.
Election officials attempted to distinguish the similarly named candidates on Tuesday’s ballot by identifying Dan S. Sullivan as the Republican incumbent while listing his opponent as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. without a party affiliation.
This article may contain commentary which reflects the author's opinion.

sources.text:
Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-AK) and incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK) are set to face off in the general elections following Tuesday’s nonpartisan primary. The other two candidates in Alaska’s crowded 16-person Senate field have not yet been called.
As of 8 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Peltola had 48% of the vote and Sullivan had 42.8% with 80% of votes in.
The race, which could help determine party control of the Senate for the next two years, has already been filled with drama.
Former congresswoman Peltola — the biggest threat to Sullivan, fired multiple senior campaign staff days before Tuesday’s primary. One source with knowledge of the firings described the campaign as in “complete chaos,” according to the Alaska Landmine.
Peltola was first elected to Congress in a 2022 special election after Rep. Don Young (R-AK), Alaska’s longest serving House Republican, passed away. She was the first Alaska native to serve in Congress and first woman to represent the state in the House of Representatives.
Peltola served Alaska’s at-large congressional district from 2022 to 2025 before losing her reelection campaign to Rep. Nick Begich (R-AK). In January 2026, she officially launched her Senate campaign.
Dan J. Sullivan, who is also challenging the two-term senator, is another name that has garnered a lot of attention. He’d received 2.4% of the vote as of Wednesday morning.
The retired teacher entered the Senate race in May, much to the dismay of the incumbent. Senator Sullivan claimed that his similarly-named challenger was a plant brought in by Democrats and Peltola’s Senate campaign to confuse voters.
“The Democrat party is talking about ‘we care about fair elections.’ It’s bullshit,” Sullivan, told a group of reporters, including TPM, in June. “The Democrats in DC, the Peltola campaign are complicit in trying to trick Alaskans — that’s an insult — to rig, and I say very strongly, rig an election in their favor.”
Shortly after, Alaska’s Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher deemed Sullivan ineligible for the primary, saying his candidacy “was not filed in good faith for the purpose of genuinely pursuing election as Alaska’s U.S. Senator.”
Sullivan challenged the decision in court, saying Beecher’s decision to disqualify him violated state and federal law.
In June, the Alaska Supreme Court sided with Sullivan, ruling that the retired teacher is qualified to run for the Senate seat and ordering state officials to place him on the primary ballot.
For the general election, Alaska will be using ranked choice voting, which allows voters to rank candidates on the ballot in order of preference regardless of their party affiliation. A candidate needs a simple majority of the vote to be declared the winner of an election. If no candidate receives a simple majority, the candidate with the least amount of votes is eliminated from running. The voters who have picked that candidate as their first choice have their votes redistributed to their second choices. This process continues until one candidate receives the majority of the votes.

sources.news_title: Alaska’s Incumbent Republican Sullivan, Democrat Peltola Advance to November Election
sources.text:
(The Center Square)–U.S. Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Mary Peltola advanced to November’s general election for U.S. Senate in Alaska’s crucial race to determine control of the upper chamber.
Alaska voters selected the incumbent Republican senator and a prominent former congresswoman as two of the top four vote getters in the state’s nonpartisan primary on Tuesday. The other two candidates were unclear by the time of publication.
Sullivan has touted his record supporting the Trump administration’s agenda, including his vote for the “One Big Beautiful Bill” and the Save America Act, signature Trump policies that are unpopular with other Alaska Republicans including Sen. Lisa Murkowski.
“I don’t think we have a big voter challenge in terms of cheating in Alaska, but for the country, there’s a place in the country where this is an important issue,” Sullivan said. “This is not focused on disenfranchising Alaska voters.”
In recent days, Sullivan ramped up his attacks on Peltola, who represented Alaska in the state’s sole U.S. House seat until she lost reelection in 2024.
Sullivan associated Peltola with Democrats in other states and accused her of attempting to play “political games.”
“Alaska is the firewall for freedom in America, and this election is too important for Alaskans to allow the political games being played by Mary Peltola and Lower 48 liberals to work,” Dan S. Sullivan said.
Peltola has focused her campaign on promoting local issues in Alaska including access to lands for fishing and bringing more oil refineries to the state. She also called for expanding solar and wind energy tax credits and eliminating the federal income tax for Alaska households earning less thatn $92,000 per year.
“Alaskans know life is harder here — but there’s only so many times you can sacrifice groceries or skip a doctor’s visit before you start to loathe the DC politicians who keep making things worse,” Peltola said. “It shouldn’t be this hard to get by in Alaska, and when I’m in the U.S. Senate, I’m going to fight to make life affordable for hardworking Alaska families.”
Peltola earned more votes than incumbent Sullivan with 61,189 as of early Wednesday morning, according to the Alaska Secretary of State. In comparison, Dan S. Sullivan earned 55,461 votes.
“Tonight shows Alaskans are fired up and ready for an independent voice in the Senate who will fix the rigged system, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” Peltola wrote on social media.
Another notable candidate in the race was Dan J. Sullivan Jr., a Republican who earned the third highest amount of votes at the time of publication with 3,147. His candidacy has been criticized and brought with legal challenges over having the same name as the incumbent Senator.
Trump slammed Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy and accused him of being aligned with Democrats in Alaska, including Peltola, to confuse voters. Dan J. Sullivan Jr. has denied any connection to Peltola or other Democrats.
“The Crooked, Radical Left Dumocrats have put up another man named ‘Dan Sullivan,’ and they did this to take away votes from our Great Senator of the same name,” Trump wrote on social media. “Democrats are trying to ‘trick’ Alaskans, and treat Alaskan Voters with contempt.”
Dan J. Sullivan Jr. has focused his campaign on criticizing the Trump administration’s cuts to federal forestry and wildlife programs in Alaska.
“We lost a lot of people. We lost a lot of programs. We lost a lot of money,” Sullivan said. “We lost a lot of scientific data that’s important to our fisheries programs.”
Dan S. Sullivan leads in fundraising with more than $7.2 million in cash on hand, followed by Peltola with more than $4.6 million, according to the Federal Election Commission.
It was still too early to tell by the time of publication who the third and fourth highest vote-getters would be in the critical election with consequences for the balance of the U.S. Senate. Republicans currently control the chamber with a 53-45 makeup, while two independent members caucus with Democrats.
Democrats see Alaska as a prime opportunity to flip seats in the chamber. The Cook Political Report ranks Alaska’s U.S. Senate race as one of four “toss up” elections.
Two Storms, One Harvest
Every food crisis in living memory has been a one-shock event. The 2008 price spike was a commodity bubble. The 2020 shortages were a logistics failure. The 2022 grain scare was a war on one exporter’s ports. Each time, the system bent, adjusted, and recovered, and each time the experts assured us afterward that global markets are simply too big and too diversified to fail.
What nobody in Washington seems eager to discuss is that 2026 is shaping up to be something the modern food system has never actually faced. Two independent shocks, one climatic and one geopolitical, are converging on the same harvest cycle at the same time. Not sequentially. Simultaneously.
Start with the weather. The Pacific Ocean is currently building toward what forecasters now openly call a record event. NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center puts the odds of at least a strong El Niño near 88 percent, with roughly two in three odds it reaches “very strong” status, the tier reserved for perhaps three or four events in the entire satellite era. Every major global model now projects a median peak in Super El Niño territory, and most of them project it exceeding the 2015-16 event, which until now held the modern record. Sea surface anomalies were already brushing the super threshold in mid-July, months before these events normally peak. The atmosphere has already shifted into El Niño mode, and the event is forecast to crest in late fall and early winter.
This is not about “climate change.” It’s about the standard cycles of weather, and the cycle we’re currently in is one that has likely devastated societies in the past. We’re better prepared as a society today, but not all Americans are equally prepared.
Serious households have started doing the quiet math on their own. Grocery bills tell part of the story, and the forecast maps tell the rest, which is why long-term food storage has moved from fringe hobby to mainstream line item in the family budget, with established suppliers like Heaven’s Harvest seeing demand from people who five years ago would have rolled their eyes at the idea. That instinct is not paranoia. It is pattern recognition, and the pattern is worth walking through carefully.

The Fertilizer Clock Is Already Running
While the Pacific warms, the second shock has been unfolding in the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict with Iran turned the world’s most important energy chokepoint into a contested waterway, and the consequences reach far beyond the gas pump. Roughly a third of global fertilizer trade moves through Hormuz, and the disruption sent urea prices up 86 percent year over year by March, with a 53 percent jump in a single month.
The World Bank projects energy prices rising about 24 percent in 2026 and fertilizer about 31 percent. By its own accounting, fertilizer prices ran 35 percent higher in the first five months of this year than the same period last year.
Here is the mechanism the nightly news will not explain. Fertilizer is not a grocery item. It is a time-delayed input. The nitrogen a farmer in Iowa or Punjab could not afford to apply this spring does not show up as a problem this spring. It shows up as a thinner harvest six to twelve months later.
The World Bank’s own food security brief concedes that the effects of reduced applications earlier this season “are likely to become visible only later in harvest outcomes.” Translate that from institutional language into plain English and it means this. The damage is already done, it is already in the ground, and we are simply waiting for it to arrive on the shelf.
Now check the calendar. Six to twelve months from the spring planting season lands us squarely in late 2026 and early 2027. Which is precisely when the strongest El Niño in the instrumental record is forecast to peak, bringing its signature droughts to Southeast Asia, Australia, southern Africa, northern Brazil, and South Asia, the very regions that grow the world’s rice, sugar, and oilseeds.
The World Bank warns openly that a strong El Niño “could disrupt multiple crop belts simultaneously” on top of the conflict-driven input costs. Their baseline projection assumes the Middle East disruptions ease by autumn. What in the last two years of Middle East history suggests that assumption is safe?
The System Has No Slack Left
The comfortable answer is that global markets always adjust. But adjustment requires slack, and the slack is gone. Global cereal production is expected to decline from last year’s records even before El Niño does its work. The UN World Food Programme, hardly a den of right-wing preppers, is calling this the most significant disruption to its supply chains since Covid and the invasion of Ukraine, and its supply chain director put the stakes bluntly.
Today’s supply chain challenges are tomorrow’s hunger crisis.
There is also a political dimension that markets cannot price. When food gets scarce, governments do not behave like economists. They behave like politicians. Export bans, hoarding mandates, and panic buying at the national level turned the modest rice shortfall of 2008 into a global crisis, and analysts are already warning that import-dependent nations are the first dominoes.
The 2015-16 Super El Niño, a far weaker event than what is now forecast, threw tens of millions into food stress across Africa and Asia. This one is projected to be stronger, and it arrives with fertilizer already rationed by price and shipping lanes already contested by missiles.
What Joseph Knew
Scripture does not treat preparation for lean years as faithlessness. It treats it as wisdom delivered in advance to those willing to act on it.
Behold, there come seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt: And there shall arise after them seven years of famine; and all the plenty shall be forgotten in the land of Egypt.
Joseph did not respond to that warning with a hashtag or a committee. He stored grain during the years of abundance, and when the famine came, Egypt stood while its neighbors begged. The lesson is not that famine is certain. It is that the time to prepare is precisely when preparation still looks optional.
Nobody who filled a pantry in a year of plenty has ever regretted it, and nobody standing in an empty aisle has ever been glad he waited for certainty.
None of this calls for panic, and panic is the enemy of sound judgment anyway. It calls for the same unglamorous prudence our grandparents considered ordinary. Keep some cash margin, know your local growers, and put real food in deep storage while it is cheap and available, because the entire arc of this story is that cheap and available is a closing window.

With midterm dynamics traditionally boosting the party opposing the White House, Democrats are hoping Peltola, who's billed herself as an independent voice for Alaskans, can flip the seat in this year's election, getting them one step closer to taking control of the chamber.

JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former Rep. The Senate race was one of several being decided in Tuesday’s primary, which also featured Alaska’s only U.S. House seat and a wide open governor’s race. Under the state’s open primary system, all candidates appeared on the same ballot. The four top vote-getters qualify for the ranked vote general election, but it was too early to call all candidates advancing in the top races.
In the House race, Republican Rep. Nick Begich advanced, along with independent Bill Hill. Two Democrats, former lawmakers Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Tom Begich, Nick Begich’s uncle, advanced in the race for governor.

Senate race features 2 widely known candidates
Sullivan and Peltola were the highest-profile candidates among a field of 16 and vastly outraised the other competitors. The race, among a handful that could help determine control of the Senate, has drawn significant attention from outside groups, with Republican and Democratic campaign organizations identifying it as a top target.
Peltola, who in 2022 became the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress, has tried to steer a centrist path and revived the “fish, family, freedom” slogan that first propelled her to office. But in the days before the primary, she shook up her campaign leadership. The campaign described the changes as “staffing updates as we transition into the general election.”
Sullivan, a veteran and ally of President Donald Trump who is seeking a third term, campaigned on supporting the military, opening more land for oil and gas extraction, and voting for Trump’s signature tax and spending law. He told supporters Tuesday that his office is “getting big things done.”
He said “D.C. Democrats” don’t have a vision for the state but instead have placed a target on Alaska, such as opposing opening the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil drilling.
He criticized Peltola as ineffective during her time in Congress. She lost reelection in 2024.
Peltola said she worked well with Sullivan as part of the state’s three-person congressional delegation. But she said the Trump administration has brought challenges to Alaska, including cuts to the federal workforce, and she blasted Sullivan for his support of Trump’s tax and spending bill. She said the bill has not brought opportunity to Alaskans and accused Sullivan of voting for “corporate greed.”
“We’ve got to get working people — regular people — in” office, she told supporters.
A second Dan Sullivan garnered attention
A third candidate, a Republican also named Dan Sullivan, stole much of the attention ahead of the primary.
Dan J. Sullivan won a legal fight to appear on the ballot despite claims by the senator and GOP allies that he was a sham candidate running at the behest of Democrats with the intent of causing confusion. Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher from the island community of Petersburg, denied that and said frustration with the incumbent prompted him to run.
He appeared on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation — a decision that a state elections official said was intended to minimize possible confusion. The senator was listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent.
It was too early to determine whether he would be among the four Senate candidates in the general election.
Matchups in House, governor’s races still taking shape
Nick Begich, who was endorsed by Trump, cast himself as hardworking and effective in his role in the U.S. House. He said results from the primary show that Alaskans are ready to return him to Congress.
Hill, a fisherman and former educator from a small southwestern village, has made affordability a key issue in his campaign. He said Alaskans are tired of paying high costs for healthcare, gas and groceries.
“Begich and his buddies think they can play by a different set of rules than we do,” he said after advancing Tuesday. “The Alaskans I know don’t think that’s right.”
The governor’s race was wide open with Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy barred by term limits from seeking a third consecutive stint. The crowded field was mostly led by Republican tickets. A Democrat hasn’t served as governor in Alaska since Tony Knowles left office in 2002.
Republicans in the race included Bernadette Wilson, a businessperson and conservative activist; Click Bishop, a former lawmaker; Dave Bronson, a former mayor of Anchorage; and Adam Crum and Treg Taylor, two former members of Dunleavy’s Cabinet.

Sullivan and Peltola have raised by far the most money to date in the race and have the greatest name recognition across Alaska, making them the leading contenders in November.
In the race for the state’s lone U.S. House seat, Republican Rep. Nick Begich advanced to the general election along with independent Bill Hill.
The campaign featured over a dozen contenders in each of the top races — for Senate, U.S. House and governor. Under Alaska’s open primary system, all candidates appeared on the same ballot, and the four who receive the most votes qualify for the ranked vote general election. It was too early to call all candidates advancing in the top races under the top-four format.
Tuesday's ballot also included state legislative candidates and a ballot initiative that would reimpose campaign contribution limits in state and local elections.
Senate race will feature 2 candidates widely known in Alaska
The highest-profile candidates in a field of 16 were Sen. Sullivan, a two-term Republican, and Peltola.
The race, which is among a handful that could help determine control of the Senate, drew significant attention from outside groups, with Republican and Democratic campaign organizations identifying it as a top target.
Peltola shook up her campaign leadership days before the primary, letting her campaign manager go and elevating a deputy to that role. In a statement, the campaign described the changes as “staffing updates as we transition into the general election.”
Sullivan, a veteran and ally of President Donald Trump, campaigned on supporting the military, opening more land for oil and gas extraction, and voting for Trump's signature tax and spending law. He told supporters Tuesday that his office is “getting big things done.”
He criticized Peltola as ineffective during her time in Congress, which spanned just over one term.
Peltola, who was elected in 2022, criticized a political system she said is rigged by special interests and allows politicians to enrich themselves. She said the Trump administration has brought challenges to Alaska including cuts to the federal workforce, and she blasted Sullivan for his support of Trump's tax and spending bill.
“We really need a champion for us in Washington, D.C., who gets us and will work hard for us,” Peltola told supporters Tuesday.
A second Dan Sullivan made a stir ahead of the primary
It was a third candidate, a Republican also named Dan Sullivan, who garnered much of the attention during the campaign.
Dan J. Sullivan won a legal fight to appear on the ballot despite claims by the senator and GOP allies that he was a sham candidate running at the behest of Democrats with the intent of causing confusion. Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher from the island community of Petersburg, denied that and said frustration with the incumbent prompted him to run.
He appeared on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation — a decision that a state elections official said was intended to minimize possible confusion. Meanwhile the senator was listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent. No other candidate seeking reelection had the “incumbent” label.
The drama involving the dueling Dan Sullivans caught the attention of Trump. In a social media post reiterating his support for the senator days before the primary, Trump called the other's candidacy an attempt to trick voters and urged his followers to vote for “SULLIVAN, DAN S.”
Dan J. Sullivan criticized the senator for embracing Trump's endorsement, calling the president “more interested in raising tariffs on our allies than in lowering the cost of groceries, housing and energy” and “more interested in punishing his enemies than bringing Americans together.”
Some voters tired of status quo, worried about shifting politics
The Senate race was a focal point for a number of voters.
Jeri Kissner said Congress must do more to push back against Trump.
“I’m so disappointed in our Congress to acquiesce to the president and his minions,” Kissner said. She favored Peltola because she did not like the other options.
Tom Dienst, who voted early and described himself as an “extremely staunch Reagan Republican,” said Trump needs allies to help carry out his agenda.
“When you look at all of the good Trump policies that will help the state, there’s just no doubt. We have to continue with Sullivan,” he said.
Republican Begich faced challenge from independent fisherman

Hill made affordability a key issue in his campaign. He said Alaskans are sick of paying high costs for healthcare, gas and groceries.
“Begich and his buddies think they can play by a different set of rules than we do,” he said after advancing Tuesday. “The Alaskans I know don’t think that’s right.”
Begich, who was endorsed by Trump, cast himself as hardworking and effective in his role. He said results from the primary show that Alaskans are ready to return him to Congress.
Progressive Democrat Matt Schultz suspended his campaign last month but remained on the ballot. His campaign said Schultz would withdraw as a general election candidate if he makes the primary’s top four. Schultz urged support for Hill.

The campaign for the state’s top executive office was an open race this year because Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy was barred by term limits from seeking a third consecutive stint.

Republicans in the race included Bernadette Wilson, a businessperson and conservative activist; Click Bishop, a former state labor commissioner and lawmaker; Dave Bronson, former mayor of Anchorage; and Adam Crum and Treg Taylor, two former members of Dunleavy's Cabinet.
Former Gov. Bill Walker, an independent, also was on the ballot.

Voters overwhelming approved the lone ballot measure at stake, which asked them to reimpose campaign contribution limits, five years after a divided federal appeals court struck down a number of caps.

Sullivan and Peltola are the leading candidates in a race that’s seen as an opportunity for Democrats hoping to take back control of the U.S. Senate, if Peltola can oust Sullivan.

The race has seen enormous fundraising by those two candidates, shadowy spending by political action committees to boost fringe candidates including non-Alaskans, and the controversial candidacy of Dan J. Sullivan, who also filed to run as a Republican.
President Donald Trump last week issued a statement urging Alaskans to not be fooled into voting for the senator’s namesake challenger, Daniel J. Sullivan, and instead to vote for Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, whom Trump said has done a “fantastic job” representing Alaska.
News also broke over the weekend that Peltola recently reorganized top staffers after she rejected the fundraising support of Kamala Harris, the Democratic presidential candidate who lost to in 2024, including by 13 points in Alaska.

Peltola’s running on what she describes as a pro-fish, pro-family campaign that focuses on affordability issues amid persistent inflation, fixing the “rigged” political system in D.C., and restoring Alaska’s struggling fisheries in part by banning factory trawling to reduce bycatch.

Sullivan said in an interview afterward that the night was early, and that in 2024, Peltola “won 51% of the vote on primary night two years ago, and then she lost.”
Earlier in the day, while campaigning in Midtown Anchorage, he weighed in on the candidacy of Petersburg’s Dan J. Sullivan, which he described as an “insult” to Alaskans. The senator and national Republicans have alleged that the Petersburg challenger is a Democratic plant trying to steal votes from the incumbent.
Dan J. Sullivan has denied those allegations, and he was allowed to appear on the Alaska ballot after the Alaska Supreme Court upheld a lower court judge’s determination that the Petersburg Sullivan was eligible to run.
“So the decoy Dan thing is a distraction, but I actually think it’s going to help us because people are mad about it,” Sen. Sullivan said.
Referring to the two years and 3.5 months Peltola served, he said she had “two terms in Congress, zero bills signed into law.”
Sullivan said he’s had dozens of bills “signed into law, and that doesn’t even include the Working Families Tax Cuts Act from last year, (in) which Alaska dominated, right?” he said, referring to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that included additional federal funds for Alaska.
Peltola on Tuesday blasted Sullivan for voting “along with corporate greed” that she blamed for crushing costs across Alaska, from “healthcare to fuel to groceries to transportation to heat.”
“And then it was the Big Beautiful Bill,” which she said “Dan Sullivan has the audacity to call this the Alaska Opportunity Act.

The race has been marked by fringe candidates who have gotten a boost with help from shadowy political action committees.
Peltola’s recently campaign committee launched a website — theyarenotfromhere.com — arguing that national Republicans were spending big to promote spoiler candidates.

sources.text:
Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK) and former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola advanced from Alaska’s crowded primary Tuesday, setting up the next phase of one of the most closely watched Senate battles of the midterm elections.
Sullivan and Peltola emerged from a 16-candidate field under Alaska’s nonpartisan primary system, in which candidates from all parties compete on the same ballot and the top four vote-getters advance to the November general election.
Recommended Stories
Shortly before 2 a.m. Eastern Time, with 50% of the vote counted, Peltola had 45.9% of the vote compared with Sullivan’s 45%, according to the Associated Press.
Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. and Gerald L. Heikes were in position to claim the remaining two spots in the general election. However, the remaining two spots remained too early to call at the time of this article’s publication. This means that two candidates named Dan Sullivan will appear on the November ballot.
Both Sullivan and Peltola were widely expected to proceed to the general election, but their respective shares of the vote could offer an early indication of the competitiveness of a race that has attracted millions of dollars in outside spending and could help determine control of the Senate.
Polling ahead of the primary showed a tight race between the two leading candidates. A New York Times-Siena University poll conducted in July showed Sullivan narrowly leading Peltola 47% to 45%, a result within the poll’s margin of error.
Other surveys have shown Peltola with a slight advantage. Alaska Survey Research found Peltola leading Sullivan 49% to 44% in March and 49% to 43% in April.
The competitive polling has helped put Alaska firmly on the national Senate map. The Cook Political Report rates the race a “toss up” as Democrats look to Alaska as one of their opportunities to gain the four seats needed to take control of the Senate.
Peltola has sought to keep some distance from the national Democratic Party as she campaigns in a state that President Donald Trump carried by 13 points in 2024. That approach was on display last week when Peltola’s campaign rejected an unsolicited fundraising appeal from former Vice President Kamala Harris. Harris’s political action committee sent an email urging supporters to donate to Peltola, describing her as key to helping Democrats regain control of the Senate. Peltola’s campaign said she was not seeking endorsements from figures outside Alaska and remained focused on the state.
National Republicans have increasingly invested in defending Sullivan. The Senate Leadership Fund announced this month that it would spend another $2 million in Alaska, bringing its total investment in the race against Peltola to $17 million.
Outside groups have also spent more than $2 million promoting little-known or perennial candidates in an effort to influence which candidates claim the remaining two spots in the top four and shape the field Sullivan and Peltola could face in November.
Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system could limit the effect of those efforts. In November, voters will rank the four candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives a majority of first-choice votes, the lowest-performing candidate will be eliminated and those ballots redistributed according to voters’ subsequent choices. The process continues until one candidate surpasses 50%.
Tuesday’s primary also included an unusual twist: Sullivan shared the ballot with another Republican candidate named Dan Sullivan.
The second Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher and former U.S. Forest Service employee, was allowed to remain on the ballot after a judge rejected an effort by the incumbent senator to have him removed.
The primary is only the opening round of a race expected to receive intense national attention over the next three months. Peltola is seeking to unseat Sullivan in a state that has traditionally favored Republicans in federal elections but where she has already demonstrated an ability to win statewide.
ALASKA SENATE ELECTION POLLS SHOW NAIL-BITER RACE BETWEEN MARY PELTOLA AND DAN SULLIVAN
Peltola won Alaska’s at-large House seat in a 2022 special election and won a full term later that year before losing reelection in 2024. For Sullivan, Tuesday’s result marked the beginning of his bid to secure another six-year term in the Senate.
The November contest is expected to be among a small number of races that could determine control of the Senate, making the primary results an early test of the coalitions Sullivan and Peltola will need to assemble this fall.

National Democrats have focused on Alaska’s federal races as they attempt to win control of Congress in this year’s midterm elections. Control of the House and Senate depend on a relative handful of seats nationally, and Alaska’s delegation could be a decisive factor.
Vote-counting is expected to continue through Aug. 28, the deadline for mailed absentee ballots to reach the Alaska Division of Elections.
Candidates who finish in the top four may also withdraw from the election until Aug. 31. If a candidate withdraws, their position is taken by the fifth-place finisher. If two candidates withdraw, the sixth-place finisher is also promoted.

“I am proud of my record as your U.S. Senator,” he said. “When I ran in 2014, I talked about getting big things done, historic things done, for our state, and that’s what we’re doing,” he said.

“D.C. Democrats don’t have an agenda or a vision for Alaska. They have a target on Alaska, and we’re not going to let them do it,” he said.
Sullivan criticized campaign spending from outside of Alaska to support his main challenger, Peltola.
“My opponent, the Democrat, she’s got unlimited money from Lower 48 billionaires and millionaires, and, you know, who the hell ever,” he said. “We don’t have that money, right? But we got you, and we’re going to win the general election with you.”
Across town, Peltola supporters gathered at a campaign event at a downtown Anchorage brewery, where she arrived just after 9 p.m. to applause from the crowd. She cited his support of the Trump administration’s Department of Government Efficiency, which fired federal employees, and his votes to defund public media and support the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which will cut nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid over the next decade.
“We have tens of thousands of Alaskans who can no longer afford health insurance, and we are getting crushed by corporate greed,” she said. “Dan Sullivan, every single vote, votes along with corporate greed. He is there for every fat cat in the nation.”
Peltola criticized the overrepresentation of millionaires and billionaires in Congress. “Half of Congress does not reflect their electorate. This has to change. We’ve got to get working people, regular people, in worrying about regular people,” she said.
She thanked her supporters and some 10,000 volunteers for her campaign and said the focus now is on the general election.
“I am so glad that the primary is now behind us. It’s a real campaign now. We are really in this,” she said. “There’s still 77 days left till November 3, and we are now in 5th gear overdrive.”

Mary Peltola, a Democrat and former U.S. representative, emerged from Alaska’s open primary on Aug. 18 as the frontrunner in the U.S. Senate race, a contest that could shift the balance of power in Congress.
The seat is held by two-term incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R-Alaska), who also advanced to the general election ballot.
The Alaska Senate race is one of five that election watchers have called a toss-up.
A win by Peltola in the general election could help place the Senate under Democratic control. Republicans currently hold a three-seat majority.
Mark Begich, whom Sullivan defeated in 2014, was the only Democrat to represent Alaska in the Senate since 1981.
Under Alaska’s election rules, the top four contenders from the non-partisan primary advance to the general election, which is decided by ranked-choice voting.
Two other candidates will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot along with Peltola and Sullivan, but they have not yet been called.
Name Controversy
Peltola led pre-election polling by up to 15 percentage points according to Real Clear Politics.
However, Sullivan may have been hampered by identity confusion as fellow Republican Dan J. Sullivan also appeared on the ballot.
Amid complaints about possible ballot confusion, Lt. Gov. Carol Beecher, who oversees elections, disqualified Dan J. Sullivan on June 11.
Beecher cited the fact that Dan J. Sullivan had never before appeared to use the shortened version of his name, Daniel, had not been affiliated with the Republican Party until two days before filing his candidacy, and had created a campaign website with branding similar to that of Dan S. Sullivan.
A judge later ruled that Dan S. Sullivan must remain on the ballot, and that ruling was subsequently upheld by the state Supreme Court.
“Every qualified citizen should have the opportunity to seek public office. Our democracy is strongest when voters have choices and when elections are decided by the people, not parties or government officials,” Dan J. Sullivan stated in campaign materials.
A spokesperson for Peltola told Reuters her campaign had no involvement with the Dan J. Sullivan candidacy.
Thirteen other candidates also appeared on the primary ballot.
Lead Contenders
Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R-Alaska), 61, has served in the Senate since 2015. He’s an attorney, a former Marine Corps officer, and a former state attorney general.
Peltola, 53, served in the U.S. House of Representatives from September 2022 to January 2025. She previously served in the Alaska House and on the Bethel City Council. She has two sons in the Coast Guard.
Peltola was a member of the Blue Dog Caucus, a group of moderate House Democrats.
Peltola outraised and outspent her principal opponent as of July 29, the last campaign finance reporting deadline before the election.
She had raised about $19 million and spent nearly $14 million to Dan S. Sullivan’s $12 million raised and $5 million spent by that date.
Candidate spending in Alaska’s 2022 senatorial campaign totaled about $18 million, according to information compiled by Ballotopedia.
Alaska First Messaging
Both candidates ran statewide media campaigns that primarily emphasized their biographies. Both aimed to portray themselves as standing with Alaskans against outside influences.
“It was an honor to serve our country in uniform. And it’s an honor to fight for Alaska in the U.S. Senate,” Sen. Dan Sullivan said in one video ad.
He stressed the importance of fighting for something bigger than oneself, accompanied by text stating that Peltola had sold out U.S. troops by voting against a pay increase.
A second ad featured a testimonial from a disabled Marine Corps veteran, crediting Sullivan for helping him obtain needed healthcare services without having to leave the state.
Peltola emphasized her status as a lifelong Alaskan in a first ad, stating, “When I think of an Alaskan I think about somebody who has a genuine connection to the land and the people and the experience of living and growing and raising a family.”
In a second ad, Peltola stated, “There is nobody more dedicated to our veterans and military families than a military mom.”
The ad touts her voting record, which she said includes approving a large pay increase for members of the military.
Key Issue: Bycatch
The protection of Alaska’s fishing industry emerged as a key issue in the campaign.
Political action committees have run ads for and against the candidates on the issue of bycatch, which is the unintended catch of certain fish and other marine life while trawling.
Both Peltola and Sullivan have opposed practices such as bottom trawling, which produce high rates of bycatch.
Sullivan introduced a bill to limit the practices, and Peltola published an op-ed in the Anchorage Daily News calling for a ban on factory trawling.
Two political action committees, Right For Alaska and Fair Deal Alaska, spent about $1.3 million in advertising either for Sen. Dan Sullivan or against Peltola between July 20 and Aug. 17, according to Federal Election Commission records.

The campaign featured over a dozen contenders in each of the top races — for Senate, U.S. House and governor. Under Alaska’s open primary system, all candidates appeared on the same ballot, and the four who receive the most votes qualify for the ranked vote general election. It was too early to call all candidates advancing in the top races under the top-four format.
Tuesday's ballot also included state legislative candidates and a ballot initiative that would reimpose campaign contribution limits in state and local elections.
Senate race will feature 2 candidates widely known in Alaska
The highest-profile candidates in a field of 16 were Sen. Sullivan, a two-term Republican, and Peltola.
The race, which is among a handful that could help determine control of the Senate, drew significant attention from outside groups, with Republican and Democratic campaign organizations identifying it as a top target.
Peltola shook up her campaign leadership days before the primary, letting her campaign manager go and elevating a deputy to that role. In a statement, the campaign described the changes as “staffing updates as we transition into the general election.”
Sullivan, a veteran and ally of President Donald Trump, campaigned on supporting the military, opening more land for oil and gas extraction, and voting for Trump's signature tax and spending law. He told supporters Tuesday that his office is “getting big things done.”
He criticized Peltola as ineffective during her time in Congress, which spanned just over one term.
Peltola, who was elected in 2022, criticized a political system she said is rigged by special interests and allows politicians to enrich themselves. She said the Trump administration has brought challenges to Alaska including cuts to the federal workforce, and she blasted Sullivan for his support of Trump's tax and spending bill.
“We really need a champion for us in Washington, D.C., who gets us and will work hard for us,” Peltola told supporters Tuesday.
A second Dan Sullivan made a stir ahead of the primary
It was a third candidate, a Republican also named Dan Sullivan, who garnered much of the attention during the campaign.
Dan J. Sullivan won a legal fight to appear on the ballot despite claims by the senator and GOP allies that he was a sham candidate running at the behest of Democrats with the intent of causing confusion. Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher from the island community of Petersburg, denied that and said frustration with the incumbent prompted him to run.
He appeared on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation — a decision that a state elections official said was intended to minimize possible confusion. Meanwhile the senator was listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent. No other candidate seeking reelection had the “incumbent” label.
The drama involving the dueling Dan Sullivans caught the attention of Trump. In a social media post reiterating his support for the senator days before the primary, Trump called the other's candidacy an attempt to trick voters and urged his followers to vote for “SULLIVAN, DAN S.”
Dan J. Sullivan criticized the senator for embracing Trump's endorsement, calling the president “more interested in raising tariffs on our allies than in lowering the cost of groceries, housing and energy” and “more interested in punishing his enemies than bringing Americans together.”
Some voters tired of status quo, worried about shifting politics
The Senate race was a focal point for a number of voters.
Jeri Kissner said Congress must do more to push back against Trump.
“I’m so disappointed in our Congress to acquiesce to the president and his minions,” Kissner said. She favored Peltola because she did not like the other options.
Tom Dienst, who voted early and described himself as an “extremely staunch Reagan Republican,” said Trump needs allies to help carry out his agenda.
“When you look at all of the good Trump policies that will help the state, there’s just no doubt. We have to continue with Sullivan,” he said.
Republican Begich faced challenge from independent fisherman
In the House race, the most prominent candidates were Begich, seeking a second term, and Hill, a fisherman and former educator from a small southwestern village.
Hill made affordability a key issue in his campaign. He said Alaskans are sick of paying high costs for healthcare, gas and groceries.
“Begich and his buddies think they can play by a different set of rules than we do,” he said after advancing Tuesday. “The Alaskans I know don’t think that’s right.”
Begich, who was endorsed by Trump, cast himself as hardworking and effective in his role. He said results from the primary show that Alaskans are ready to return him to Congress.
Progressive Democrat Matt Schultz suspended his campaign last month but remained on the ballot. His campaign said Schultz would withdraw as a general election candidate if he makes the primary’s top four. Schultz urged support for Hill.
Governor's race wide open
The campaign for the state’s top executive office was an open race this year because Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy was barred by term limits from seeking a third consecutive stint.
Two Democrats advanced to the general election from a crowded, largely Republican field: former state lawmakers Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Tom Begich, who is Nick Begich's uncle. If either wins in November, he would become Alaska's first Democratic governor since Tony Knowles left office in 2002.
Republicans in the race included Bernadette Wilson, a businessperson and conservative activist; Click Bishop, a former state labor commissioner and lawmaker; Dave Bronson, former mayor of Anchorage; and Adam Crum and Treg Taylor, two former members of Dunleavy's Cabinet.
Former Gov. Bill Walker, an independent, also was on the ballot.
Ballot measure addresses money in state politics
Voters overwhelming approved the lone ballot measure at stake, which asked them to reimpose campaign contribution limits, five years after a divided federal appeals court struck down a number of caps.
The measure imposes a $2,000 limit on how much individuals can give to candidates in state and local elections and a $5,000 cap on what they can give to political parties. It also limits spending by groups other than political parties and limits what individuals and groups can give to joint campaigns for governor and lieutenant governor.

Washington — GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola are among those advancing to the general election in November in Alaska’s Senate race, WTX US News projects, as Sullivan defends his seat in a race that could be key to determining control of the chamber next year.
Though Alaska hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008, Sullivan, a second-term senator and a Marine veteran who worked at the State Department under the George W. Bush administration, faces a formidable opponent in Peltola.
Peltola, 52, became the first Democrat to represent the state in the House in 50 years in 2022, though she ultimately lost her reelection bid for Alaska’s sole House seat the following cycle. But Peltola, the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress, fell short by less than 3 points in the 2024 race, despite President Trump winning the state by 13 points.
With midterm dynamics traditionally boosting the party opposing the White House, Democrats are hoping Peltola, who’s billed herself as an independent voice for Alaskans, can flip the seat in this year’s election, getting them one step closer to taking control of the chamber.
In Alaska, the top-four vote getters in the primary advance to the general election. The other two candidates have not yet been determined.
As Sen. Sullivan, 61, fights to hold onto his seat, which he last won by a comfortable margin in 2020, Republicans are investing in the contest. The Senate Leadership Fund has announced $17 million in advertising spending to boost Sullivan in the race.
On the Democratic side, the Senate Majority PAC has also invested, with more than $12 million in television reservations to support Peltola. But as Peltola is campaigning to flip the seat, she’s drawn a line between herself and one high-profile national Democrat. Peltola’s campaign rejected the support of former Vice President Kamala Harris days ahead of the primary, after Harris’ PAC sought to fundraise on her behalf.
To flip control of the Senate, where Republicans currently hold 53 seats, Democrats would have to win four seats while defending a handful of their own. The 2026 map has long been viewed as difficult for Democrats, with few opportunities for pickups. But with races like the one in Alaska, the party sees an opportunity to improve its chances.
